name: Finding Adjacent Duplicates in a Sequence of Numbers
description: Construct a program that checks whether a sequence of numbers, entered one at a time, contains adjacent duplicates. The user enters -1 to indicate the end of the input.\nFor example, 4 is a duplicate in the sequence of numbers 1, 3, 4, 4, -1.
code:
#Step 1: Read the first number that the user enters
text = input("Enter a number: ")
num = float(text)
#Step 2: Read the rest of the numbers that the user enters and check for adjacent duplicates
while num != -1 :
    previous = num
    text = input("Enter a number: ")
    num = float(text)    
    if num == previous :
        print("Duplicate input for number:", num)

commentList: You display the prompt "Enter a number: " and wait for the user to type something; the input(...) call returns the characters the user types as a string.
You assign that returned string to the variable text using =, so text now holds the raw user input for later use.
You should remember that input returns a string, not a numeric type, which is why the next line converts text to a float; a common misconception is to expect input to give you a number directly.

You can run into errors if the user types something that is not a valid number (or just presses Enter); the later float(text) will raise an error in that case, so consider validating or using try/except before conversion.
You might want to make the prompt clearer by including the sentinel (for example: "Enter a number (-1 to stop): ") and you can also call text = text.strip() before converting to remove extra spaces.

commentList: Purpose: This line converts the text you read from the user into a numeric value and stores it in the variable num so you can do numeric comparisons (like checking for the -1 sentinel and comparing adjacent numbers).

Syntax and simple breakdown: the left side (num) is a variable name, the equals sign assigns a value, and float(text) calls Python's float function to turn the string stored in text into a floating-point number.

How it works (semantics): float(text) parses the characters in text and returns a float object (for example, '4' becomes 4.0). That float is then assigned to num so later comparisons like num != -1 and num == previous work as numeric checks, not string checks.

Common errors and misconceptions: input() returns a string, not a number — if you skip this conversion and compare strings you'll get wrong results. Also float(text) will raise a ValueError if the user types something that isn't a valid number (like 'four' or '3,5').

Best practices: wrap this conversion in a try/except block to catch invalid input and ask the user again. If you only want whole numbers, consider int(text) instead. Also be consistent with the sentinel type (using -1 or -1.0 is fine because Python compares ints and floats by value).

A note about equality: comparing float values for equality can be risky after arithmetic, but here you're converting direct user input (e.g., '-1' → -1.0), so checking num == -1 will work as expected.

commentList: Purpose: This line starts a loop that keeps reading and checking numbers as long as the current number is not the end-of-input marker -1. It controls the repeated checking for adjacent duplicates.
Syntax and meaning: 'while' begins a loop, 'num != -1' is the loop condition meaning 'continue while num is not equal to -1', and the ':' starts the indented block that runs each iteration.
Pre-check behavior: The condition is tested before each iteration. If the first number you read is -1, the loop body will not run and no duplicate checks will be performed.
Update requirement: For the loop to finish, you must change num inside the loop (Line 8 does this). If you forget to update num, the condition stays true and you get an infinite loop.

Type and comparison caution: num is a float here; comparing it to -1 (an int) works in Python (e.g. -1 == -1.0). However, if you accidentally compare the raw input string to -1 or use floating-point results from calculations, equality checks can be incorrect or fail.

Common error to watch for: If input conversion to float fails (non-numeric text), you'll get a ValueError before reaching the loop body. You should validate or handle exceptions if you expect bad input.

Best practice: Avoid magic numbers — consider naming the sentinel (e.g., SENTINEL = -1) or clearly comment its role. Another common pattern is using 'while True' with an explicit 'break' when you see the sentinel; both approaches are fine if you keep the loop update and checks clear.

commentList: Purpose: you store the current number (num) into the variable previous so you can compare it with the next number entered and detect adjacent duplicates.
Syntax & semantics: 'previous = num' is an assignment statement — it copies the numeric value held in num into the name previous. For immutable numbers this creates a snapshot of the value.
How it fits the logic: by saving the current value before you read the next input, you implement a sliding 'one-step' comparison: after you read the next num you can test if num == previous.
Common mistake: if you forget to read and set num before entering the loop, previous = num will raise a NameError because num is undefined. Make sure the initial input (Lines 2–3) runs first.
Possible confusion: '=' assigns a value; '==' compares values. If you accidentally write 'previous == num' you won't set previous and the comparison will be lost.
Sentinel note: because the loop runs only when num != -1, previous will never be the sentinel value -1. This prevents treating the sentinel as part of the data in this code structure.

Best practices: use a clearer name like previous_num or prev; validate input with try/except before assigning; and if you expect integers prefer int() to avoid float-equality issues (or use a tolerance for real numbers).

Why this line is essential: without converting to a numeric type you would be comparing strings (which can give wrong results for numeric comparisons and for values like '10' vs '10.0'), so this assignment is required for the adjacent-duplicate check to work correctly.

commentList: Purpose: This line tells the user that you found two equal numbers in a row by printing a clear message plus the actual number that was duplicated.

How it works (syntax): print() is called with two arguments: the string "Duplicate input for number:" and the variable num. print() converts num to text and inserts a space between the string and the number when it prints them.

Role in the program: This line runs only when the if condition (num == previous) is true, so it directly signals the program's success in detecting an adjacent duplicate — it is the user-facing output of the core check.

Common misconception / sentinel handling: You might worry that the sentinel -1 will be reported as a duplicate. With the current loop structure, the sentinel does not get counted as previous, so -1 will not be printed as a duplicate here.

Potential error with types: num is a float because you used float(text). That means the printed value may look like 4.0 instead of 4. If you expect whole numbers, convert to int or parse as int earlier to avoid confusing output.

Floating-point caution: Comparing floats for equality can sometimes be unreliable for non-exact decimal values (due to rounding). If users enter decimal numbers where tiny differences matter, consider a tolerance-based comparison instead of ==.

Best practice / clearer formatting: Use an f-string or explicit formatting for clearer output, for example: print(f"Duplicate input for number: {num}") or print("Duplicate input for number:", int(num)) if you want no decimal part. Also decide whether you want to stop after the first duplicate (use break) or report all duplicates (leave as is).

distractors.description: If you use while num == -1 :, you are asking the program to enter the loop only when the current number equals the sentinel. Because most inputs are not -1, the loop will usually never run and you won't read any additional numbers or check for adjacent duplicates. Conversely, if the very first number is -1, you'll enter the loop even though -1 is meant to signal end-of-input; then the code will try to treat -1 as a valid value, read more inputs, and carry on when it should stop. You might choose this because you misread the sentinel logic and think the loop should trigger on the sentinel rather than stop at it. This line flips the intended meaning of the condition and so prevents the program from terminating or continuing in the right cases.

Using while True : creates an infinite loop unless you include an explicit break inside the loop body. In the given code there is no break, so replacing the condition with while True : will cause the program to keep prompting the user forever even after they enter -1. You might pick this because you think the loop will naturally stop when num becomes -1, but without a break or a loop condition the loop control never checks that value to exit. The result is an endless series of prompts (or a program that only stops if you forcibly terminate it), so the input sentinel no longer serves its purpose.

You might choose this because the word 'is' reads naturally ("if this number is the previous one") and might seem like a good way to test sameness. Step-by-step, this uses an identity test rather than a value equality test: it checks whether the two variables refer to the exact same object in memory. For small integers you might sometimes see it appear to work because of implementation details, which can reinforce the mistaken idea that it is equivalent to an equality check. However, with floats (and in general) the identity test is not reliable for determining whether two numbers have the same value. If you use this line, the program will sometimes miss duplicates or behave inconsistently, so adjacent equal numbers might not be detected. In short, this distractor uses the wrong notion of "sameness": it checks identity instead of comparing the numeric values, which prevents the program from reliably detecting duplicates.
